A long, low, hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers me with the same call.

The sound of water is the rush of the pond at the edge of the wood. It is a low, continuous murmur, like the wind through the reeds. I hear it when I am perched on the old beech, and it reminds me of the marsh. Sometimes I think I hear the water in the distance, but it is more likely the wind. I do not like the sound of water. It is too cold and too far away. I prefer the sound of the marsh

The pond. It is a long way, but I can hear the water. It is the sound of the night: a low, continuous murmur, like the wind in the reeds. Sometimes it is louder, when the rain falls or the frogs jump in. I can tell the difference between the water and the frogs. The water is always the same, but the frogs are different. They splash and squeak. I listen for them.

The pond. It is a marshy place with reeds and frogs. I can see it from my tree, and I can hear the frogs at night. The water is still, but sometimes it ripples when the wind blows. I do not like to go near it, but I know it is there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is all grass and stone. The lane is wide and the road is wide. I see the lights of the cars at night, and the dogs that run on the road. I do not like the dogs. They bark and chase me. I fly high over the lane.

I fly low over the marsh, then up the lane, then over the pond. I look for the rustle of a mouse in the grass, or the flicker of a frog in the reeds. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait for the answer. If I don’t get one, I go back to the hollow.

It is too loud and too full of things that move without wings. I have seen a fox there once, and a badger. I do not go near the lane. I stay in the wood, where it is quiet and the air smells of earth and rain. Hoo...

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and run through the undergrowth. I hear them at night, scratching and squeaking. I sit still and wait for them to come close, then strike. They are the main thing I eat. Sometimes I catch a frog or a mouse, but voles are the most common. I can hear them under the leaves, and that's how I find them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A shrew. It is small, quick, and makes a sound like a mouse. I hear it under the leaves, and I strike. It is the first I catch in the autumn.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the marsh, the hedgerows, the lane. The long grass is where the rabbits are, but they are too fast. I wait for them to come to the edge of the marsh, where the grass is shorter. I strike at the edge of the light, where the rabbits are most vulnerable. I do not go into the long grass. I swallow whole the small things I catch. Beetles, mice, frogs, worms. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and quick. The bigger ones I tear up with my beak. I can't chew. I don't have teeth. I have a gizzard, though, and that grinds them up. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A shrew. They are small and quick, but I catch them in the undergrowth. They squeak when I pounce. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old beech. It is dark and damp, but warm. I have a nest of leaves and feathers. I sleep there, and my mate sleeps beside me. The hollow is high, so I can see the marsh and the pond and the lane. I can hear the road from there. I can hear the lane. I can hear the lane all the time.

My home is the hollow in the old beech. It is high, and the wind comes through the leaves. I can hear the wood floor creak when I move. The floor is soft, and the walls are warm. I have a nest of leaves and feathers. I am there when the night comes, and I am there when the day goes. I do not leave it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the hollow in the old beech, the one with the ivy and the moss. I made it with my mate, and we have raised our young there. The ivy is thick, and the moss keeps the cold out. I can hear the rain through the leaves, and the wind whistles through the branches. It is safe, and it is mine. I call from there at dusk, and the marsh answers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
